newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia awaits France court asset rule on Oct 1.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia awaits France court asset rule on Oct 1.

text.p: Slovenia said on Wednesday it expected a Paris court to reach a decision on October 1 on whether to keep Yugoslav assets in France frozen until the end of succession talks between the former Yugoslavia republics.
"The court, which listened to all the parties yesterday, said it would reach its decision next Tuesday," Andrej Rant, president of the management board of the Slovenian Succession Fund, told Reuters.
He said arguments in favour of keeping the assets frozen were jointly presented by the lawyers for Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia.
"It is estimated there are about $590 million of former Yugoslav assets in nine French banks," Rant said.

The banks are Societe General, Paribas, Credit Commercial de France, Banque Francaise du Commerce Exterieur, Credit Agricole, Banque Nationale de Paris, Banque Commerciale pour l'Europe du Nord, Credit Lyonnais and Banque Franco-Yugoslave.

Slovenia is involved in a similar court case in Nicosia where it is pushing for a permanent freeze of former Yugoslav assets that are held in a Yugoslav offshore bank Beogradska Banka in Cyprus and are estimated at $146 million.
According to Slovenian estimates, various banks, including the above-mentioned French and Cypriate banks, hold about $1.2 billion of the former Yugoslavia's assets.
After the break-up of Yugoslavia all assets of the former federation held by international banks were frozen in line with a United Nations resolution which expired last November.

Since then Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia have started legal procedures to keep the assets frozen until an agreement is reached on the issue of succession between the states of former Yugoslavia.

The bulk of the former federation's assets, about $660 million, is held by the Basle-based Bank for International Settlement (BIS), which recently suggested the assets should be divided according to a proposal by the International Monetary Fund which would give Slovenia a 16.39 percent stake.
Governors of the central banks of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia have all said they supported the BIS proposal, while rump Yugoslavia has so far refused to participate in the negotiations.
Rump Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, has also attempted to thwart moves by other successor repbulics to settle their shares of the former Yugoslavia's debt of $4.3 billion.
But Slovenia and Croatia have ignored legal challenges by Belgrade and completed separate debt repayment agreements with their creditors. -- Marja Novak, Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
